title: "5.7 Limitations and compensating controls"

The chapter raises six open findings about its own model and policy. Each has evidence
drawn from the facts, a compensating control and an owner. The same six, in the same
words, are D5's open findings in the validation sign-off (D11, in the validation PDF). The
model and the policy are not changed by this chapter: it documents them as committed.

## Finding 1 — On the booked, AUC is below the AUC gate value and no better than the scorecard {#adj-finding-1}

**Finding.** The model trains and is gated on all applicants. On the loans the bank books
it ranks below the value of its own AUC gate, and no better than the scorecard whose output
is its strongest input.

**Evidence.** On the held-out split ([5.5](performance.qmd#by-population)):

- all applicants, the gates' population: AUC {{< var adj.pop.everyone.auc >}}
  ({{< var adj.pop.everyone.n >}} rows) against the {{< var adj.gate_auc >}} gate; lift
  {{< var adj.pop.everyone.lift >}}× against {{< var adj.gate_lift >}}×;
- booked only: AUC {{< var adj.pop.booked.auc >}} ({{< var adj.pop.booked.n >}} rows; bootstrap
  95% interval {{< var adj.pop.booked.auc_ci_lo >}}–{{< var adj.pop.booked.auc_ci_hi >}}) —
  below the gate value; lift {{< var adj.pop.booked.lift >}}× — above it;
- the scorecard on the same booked rows: AUC {{< var score.pop.booked.auc >}}
  ([5.3](methodology.qmd#adj-why-lightgbm)).

The comparison with the scorecard is paired: both PDs are scored on the same resampled
rows in each of {{< var score.bootstrap_n >}} bootstrap resamples, so the interval is for the
difference itself. On the booked the scorecard's AUC exceeds the model's by
{{< var adj.vs_score.booked.diff >}}, with a 95% interval from
{{< var adj.vs_score.booked.lo >}} to {{< var adj.vs_score.booked.hi >}}. The interval contains zero: the model is *no better*
than the scorecard on the booked, not measurably worse. The gate value is a different matter:
the booked sample's own bootstrap interval, {{< var adj.pop.booked.auc_ci_lo >}} to
{{< var adj.pop.booked.auc_ci_hi >}}, lies wholly below {{< var adj.gate_auc >}}, so the
shortfall is not sampling noise. As in D4 (D4 finding 2), this is not a defect of the
data: the generator gives every applicant an outcome, and the gap is a property of where the
gate is measured.

**Impact.** The AUC gate overstates how well the model ranks the applicants who look like
the bank's borrowers, and the richer model does not earn its cost — SHAP reasons in place of
exact ones ([5.3](methodology.qmd#adj-reason-codes)) — on the population where lending
happens. The lift gate still passes on the booked, so the model still concentrates
defaulters among its riskiest files; what is weaker is its ordering of the rest, which is
where the Approve / Refer cutoff falls.

**Compensating control.** Report all three populations on every run (the generated table in
[5.2](data.qmd#two-populations) does); track the booked-only AUC and lift beside the gates
in monitoring ([5.8](monitoring.qmd)); at redevelopment, weigh gating on the booked
population and the alternative of placing the zones on the scorecard's PD
([5.3](methodology.qmd#alternative-considered-pd-zones-on-the-scorecards-pd)). The gates
themselves are not changed by this finding ([5.9](gate.qmd)). **Owner:** model developer.

## Finding 2 — Two policy rules can never fire on this data {#adj-finding-2}

**Finding.** The leverage knockout and the large-request override are in the policy, in
`policy_config.json` and in the workbench's rule ledger. On this data neither can ever
fire.

**Evidence.** Over all {{< var adj.n_applicants >}} applicants
([5.3](methodology.qmd#rule-hits-on-the-held-out-applicants)):

| Rule | Limit | Largest value in the data | Hits, all applicants |
|---|---|---|---|
| `leverage` knockout | leverage above {{< var adj.policy.leverage_cap >}} | {{< var adj.max_leverage >}} | {{< var adj.rule.leverage.n_all >}} |
| `large_request` override | requested amount over revenue above {{< var adj.policy.req_to_rev_cap >}} | {{< var adj.max_req_to_rev >}} | {{< var adj.rule.large_request.n_all >}} |

The generator explains both. `leverage` is total debt over annual revenue, with total debt
drawn as revenue times a uniform multiplier whose top is far below the cap; the requested
amount is revenue times a uniform multiplier whose top is below the request cap
(`shared/data_generator.py`):

```python
total_debt = np.clip(annual_revenue * rng.uniform(0.05, 0.80, n), 0, None).round(-3)
leverage = np.clip(total_debt / np.maximum(annual_revenue, 1.0), 0, 5).round(2)
requested_amount = np.clip(annual_revenue * rng.uniform(0.05, 0.50, n), 1e4, 5e6).round(-3)
```

The leverage cap is even above the generator's own clip on `leverage`. A cap of that size
reads like a debt-to-EBITDA limit applied to a debt-to-revenue ratio. Nor do the unit tests
exercise either rule: `tests/test_policy.py` tests the coverage knockout, the zones, the
thin-coverage override and the score floor, and not these two.

**Impact.** Two untested controls. A reviewer reading the configuration would take high
leverage and oversized requests to be stopped; on this data nothing is stopped by either
rule, and if the definitions of the ratios are wrong, nothing would be on a real book
either. Leverage is one of the generator's default drivers (D4.3): it reaches the decision
only through the model's PD.

**Compensating control.** At the next policy review, restate each limit on the definition of
the ratio this data uses — or remove the rule and say so — and add a unit test that makes
each rule fire. Until then, the monitoring plan reports every rule's hit rate on every cohort
and flags any rule with no hits ([5.8](monitoring.qmd#adj-rule-hits)). **Owner:** credit
policy owner.

## Finding 3 — The Approve zone under-predicts default {#adj-finding-3}

**Finding.** Among the files the model's PD places in the Approve zone, more default than
the PD predicts, by more than the calibration tolerance, on enough defaults to count — on
the held-out booked and on all held-out applicants.

**Evidence.** By PD zone, before knockouts and overrides ([5.5](performance.qmd#adj-calibration)):

- held-out booked, Approve zone: {{< var adj.zone.booked.Approve.n >}} files,
  {{< var adj.zone.booked.Approve.defaults >}} defaults, observed
  {{< var adj.zone.booked.Approve.observed >}} against predicted
  {{< var adj.zone.booked.Approve.predicted >}}: observed / predicted
  {{< var adj.zone.booked.Approve.ratio >}};
- all held-out applicants, Approve zone: {{< var adj.zone.everyone.Approve.n >}} files,
  {{< var adj.zone.everyone.Approve.defaults >}} defaults, observed
  {{< var adj.zone.everyone.Approve.observed >}} against predicted
  {{< var adj.zone.everyone.Approve.predicted >}}: observed / predicted
  {{< var adj.zone.everyone.Approve.ratio >}}.

Both are outside the tolerance of {{< var monitoring.ratio_lo >}} to
{{< var monitoring.ratio_hi >}}. The monitoring plan counts a breach only on at least
{{< var monitoring.min_band_defaults >}} defaults
([5.8](monitoring.qmd#adj-redevelopment-triggers)); both clear that floor, so the same rule
D4 applies to its bands makes them a finding at development. The pattern is consistent with
D4 finding 6 — under-prediction where the bank lends — with one difference: here the Approve
zone misses on all held-out applicants too, not only on the booked. (The booked Decline zone
misses the other way: finding 6.)

**Impact.** The PD of an approved file is too low. The decision itself is not affected —
the Approve zone is a position in the ranking, not a PD limit — but any use of the PD as a
default rate is: expected loss on approved files, a portfolio PD built from them, or a
comparison of the PD with a risk appetite stated in PD terms. Pricing takes its PD from the
scorecard (D6), not from this model, so the rate is not affected by this finding; it is
affected by D4 finding 6, which is in the same place.

**Compensating control.** At the next retrain, add a calibration step to the PD (Platt or
isotonic, fitted on rows the trees were not fitted on), then recalibrate the zones and
re-verify the gates ([5.9](gate.qmd)). Until then, monitor observed / predicted by zone on
each cohort with matured outcomes, booked and all applicants, against the floor; trigger 3
of the monitoring plan applies to it as to any zone ([5.8](monitoring.qmd#adj-redevelopment-triggers)); and
treat the PD as a ranking, not a default rate (a prohibited use, [5.1](purpose.qmd#prohibited-uses)).
**Owner:** model developer.

## Finding 4 — The zone cutoffs are taken over the held-out rows too {#adj-finding-4}

**Finding.** `train.py` sets `t_low` and `t_high` as quantiles of the model's PD over all
{{< var adj.n_applicants >}} applicants ([5.3](methodology.qmd#adj-pd-zones)). The
{{< var adj.n_test >}} held-out rows are among them, so the rows used to measure the
decisions also helped set a policy parameter.

**Evidence.** The committed cutoffs are {{< var adj.t_low >}} and {{< var adj.t_high >}}.
Taken over the training rows alone they would be {{< var adj.trainonly.t_low >}} and
{{< var adj.trainonly.t_high >}}. Re-running `decide` on the held-out applicants with those
cutoffs changes {{< var adj.trainonly.changed >}} of {{< var adj.n_test >}} decisions, and
moves the decision mix to {{< var adj.trainonly.mix.Approve >}} /
{{< var adj.trainonly.mix.Refer >}} / {{< var adj.trainonly.mix.Decline >}}, against the
committed {{< var adj.mix.Approve >}} / {{< var adj.mix.Refer >}} / {{< var adj.mix.Decline >}}
([5.6](sensitivity.qmd)). The training-only cutoffs are quantiles of in-sample PDs — the
trees were fitted on those rows — so they are not an out-of-sample recalibration either
([5.4](assumptions.qmd#adj-thresholds-are-quantiles)); they show only how much the held-out
rows moved the cutoffs.

**Impact.** Immaterial in effect: {{< var adj.trainonly.changed >}} held-out decisions, and the held-out decision
mix and outcomes in [5.5](performance.qmd) are essentially what an untouched held-out set
would show. It is a control weakness, not a performance problem: the held-out set should
play no part in any fitted value, and here it plays a small one. The gates are unaffected:
AUC and lift are measured on the PD, which the cutoffs do not touch.

**Compensating control.** At the next retrain, take the cutoffs from the training rows only,
and preferably from out-of-sample PDs (cross-validated predictions on the training rows), so
that the zones are set on PDs that behave like a new applicant's. No interim action: this
record is the control. **Owner:** model developer.

## Finding 5 — The lift function's name misstates what it measures {#adj-finding-5}

**Finding.** The lift gate is computed by `top_ventile_lift`. A ventile is a twentieth; the
function measures the top {{< var adj.lift_top_share >}}.

**Evidence.** The function cuts at the 80th percentile of the PD:

```python
def top_ventile_lift(y_true, pd_hat):                     # adjudication/src/train.py
    y = np.asarray(y_true); p = np.asarray(pd_hat)
    cut = np.quantile(p, 0.80)
    top = y[p >= cut]
    base = y.mean()
    return float(top.mean() / base) if base > 0 else 0.0
```

Measured on the function rather than read from its code — one default placed on the riskiest
of {{< var adj.lift_probe_n >}} ranked rows, so that lift is the inverse of the top group's share — the top group
is {{< var adj.lift_top_share >}} of the rows (`wiki/facts/adj_facts.py::lift_top_share`).
Everything else agrees with the measurement: the module docstring (`top-20% lift`), the
validation report, the metadata key (`top20_lift`) and `verify.py`'s own recomputation, which
cuts at the same quantile and prints `top-20% lift`.

**Impact.** None on the number: the lift and the gate are what the documentation says. The
risk is to a reviewer who reads the function name and takes the gate to be on the riskiest
twentieth — a stricter test than the one run — or who reimplements it from the name and gets
a different number.

**Compensating control.** Rename the function to what it measures at the next change to
`train.py`, with the facts and tests that import it. Until then, this record and the
generated label `Top-20% lift` in every table are the control. **Owner:** model developer.

## Finding 6 — On held-out booked loans, the Decline zone over-predicts default {#adj-finding-6}

**Finding.** Among the booked files the model's PD places in the Decline zone, fewer default
than the PD predicts, by more than the calibration tolerance, on enough defaults to count.

**Evidence.** By PD zone, before knockouts and overrides ([5.5](performance.qmd#adj-calibration)):
held-out booked, Decline zone: {{< var adj.zone.booked.Decline.n >}} files,
{{< var adj.zone.booked.Decline.defaults >}} defaults, observed
{{< var adj.zone.booked.Decline.observed >}} against predicted
{{< var adj.zone.booked.Decline.predicted >}}: observed / predicted
{{< var adj.zone.booked.Decline.ratio >}}, below the lower edge of the tolerance,
{{< var monitoring.ratio_lo >}}, on at least the {{< var monitoring.min_band_defaults >}}
defaults the monitoring floor requires. On all held-out applicants the same zone is inside the tolerance
({{< var adj.zone.everyone.Decline.ratio >}} on {{< var adj.zone.everyone.Decline.defaults >}}
defaults). The miss appears only on the booked, which points at selection, not at the model:
booking was drawn from the generator's true PD
([D2](../d2-data.qmd#two-populations-applicants-and-booked)), so the few files the bank
booked despite a Decline-zone PD are the ones whose true risk was lower than their PD says.
D4 sees the same effect in its band D on the booked (D4.5).

**Impact.** Conservative. Over-predicting risk in the Decline zone would decline files that
are safer than their PD; but knockouts already decide most Declines
([5.3](methodology.qmd#adj-knockouts-dominate)), and the booked Decline zone is
{{< var adj.zone.booked.Decline.share >}} of the held-out booked. Recalibrating the zone on
the booked would fit the bank's past booking choices, not the risk of a new applicant, who
arrives without that selection.

**Compensating control.** Monitor and explain, do not recalibrate: track the booked Decline
zone's observed / predicted on each cohort with matured outcomes, against the floor, beside
the same zone on all applicants. Read a booked-only breach as selection; a breach on all
applicants as well is a calibration problem, handled with finding 3's control
([5.8](monitoring.qmd#adj-redevelopment-triggers)). **Owner:** model developer.

## Observations {#adj-observations}

Recorded but not raised as findings. Each is policy working as written, minor on this data,
or covered by a control above, and each is re-examined at redevelopment.

| Observation | Evidence | Why not a finding | Action |
|---|---|---|---|
| Hard knockouts decide most Declines | {{< var adj.decline.knockout_share >}} of the {{< var adj.decline.n >}} held-out Declines carry a knockout; knockouts overturn the PD zone on {{< var adj.rule.knockout_overturns.n >}} held-out files ([5.3](methodology.qmd#adj-knockouts-dominate)) | The knockouts are credit policy, applied as written; the decisions rank against outcomes ([5.5](performance.qmd#adj-decisions-and-outcomes)) | Read the gates as gates on the PD, not on the decision; monitor the knockout share of Declines ([5.8](monitoring.qmd#adj-rule-hits)) |
| The top SHAP reasons on Declines are the score | `{{< var adj.decline.shap1.feature >}}` in {{< var adj.decline.shap1.share >}} and `{{< var adj.decline.shap2.feature >}}` in {{< var adj.decline.shap2.share >}} of held-out Declines' top three; the two are one signal ([5.5](performance.qmd#adj-reasons-among-declines)) | A correct attribution of what the model uses; the dependency on D4 is documented (D3) | Give applicant-facing reasons from the score's own exact codes where a SHAP reason is the score; weigh dropping one of the two columns at redevelopment |
| No calibration miss below the floor | Every zone outside the tolerance rests on at least {{< var monitoring.min_band_defaults >}} defaults, and all are in findings 3 and 6 ([5.5](performance.qmd#adj-calibration)) | Nothing to record below the floor on this data | Zones below the floor on a future cohort are watched, not acted on ([5.8](monitoring.qmd#adj-redevelopment-triggers)) |
| A missing input is scored as zero, and a zero coverage ratio is a knockout | `compute_adjudication_features` fills missing numeric features with zero; `decide` fills a missing `dscr`, leverage, public records or delinquencies with zero too (a missing `business_score` defaults to the score floor, and revenue is floored at 1); `dscr` of zero is below the floor ([5.6](sensitivity.qmd#reduced-input-refits-not-run)) | The generated data have no missing values | Refer incomplete applications in any production use, rather than decline them for a reason that is not true |
| The v1 adjudication endpoint gives some Declines no reason at all | `/api/adjudicate/{business_id}` returns rule hits only. The {{< var adj.decline.no_reason.n >}} held-out Declines ({{< var adj.decline.no_reason.share >}}) decided by the PD zone alone carry an empty rule-hit list there: a Decline with no stated reason ([5.1](purpose.qmd#who-consumes-it-and-how)) | Not a defect of the model or the decision: the v2 workbench serves the full SHAP ledger for those files, and the v1 endpoint is a portfolio view, not an adverse-action channel. Raised as a finding the moment v1 is used to notify an applicant | Any adverse-action use takes its reasons from the workbench's decision view; adding the top adverse SHAP reasons to the v1 response is the fix if v1 is ever used that way |
